solution_overview:
A factory inspects finished units for three defect types: Crack ($C$), Discoloration ($D$), and Warp ($W$). We are given the probabilities of individual defects, pairwise defects, and all three defects. These probabilities are modeled as events in a sample space.

The given probabilities are:
$P(C) = 0.18$
$P(D) = 0.22$
$P(W) = 0.15$

The probabilities of units having two specific defects are:
$P(C \cap D) = 0.06$
$P(C \cap W) = 0.05$
$P(D \cap W) = 0.04$

The probability of units having all three defects is:
$P(C \cap D \cap W) = 0.015$

These values will be used to calculate probabilities of compound events.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The probability that a unit has at least one defect means the unit has a Crack OR Discoloration OR Warp. We use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events:

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - P(C \cap D) - P(C \cap W) - P(D \cap W) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substitute the given probabilities:

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - 0.06 - 0.05 - 0.04 + 0.015$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.55 - 0.15 + 0.015$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.40 + 0.015$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.415$$

Since $0.415 = 41.5\%$, and $41.5\% < 43\%$, the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The probability that the unit has exactly one defect type is the sum of probabilities of having only $C$, only $D$, or only $W$. This can be calculated from the given probabilities using a common formula derived from a Venn diagram:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - 2P(C \cap D) - 2P(C \cap W) - 2P(D \cap W) + 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substitute the given values into the formula:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - 2(0.06) - 2(0.05) - 2(0.04) + 3(0.015)$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.55 - 0.12 - 0.10 - 0.08 + 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.55 - 0.30 + 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.25 + 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.295$$

Since $0.295 = 29.5\%$, and $29.5\% \not> 30\%$, the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The probability that the unit has exactly two defect types means the unit has (Crack AND Discoloration AND NOT Warp) OR (Crack AND Warp AND NOT Discoloration) OR (Discoloration AND Warp AND NOT Crack). This can be calculated by summing the pairwise intersection probabilities and subtracting three times the triple intersection probability, as the triple intersection is included in each pairwise intersection:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W) - 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substitute the given probabilities:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04 - 3(0.015)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.15 - 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.105$$

Since $0.105 = 10.5\%$, and $10.5\% \ge 10\%$, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The probability that the unit has no defects is the complement of having at least one defect. From part A, we found the probability of having at least one defect, $P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.415$.

$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - P(C \cup D \cup W)$$
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - 0.415$$
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 0.585$$

Since $0.585 = 58.5\%$, and $58.5\% \not< 58\%$, the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The event of having at least two defect types means the unit has exactly two defects or exactly three defects. We already calculated the probability of exactly two defects in part C as $P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.105$, and the problem states the probability of exactly three defects is $P(C \cap D \cap W) = 0.015$.

$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.105 + 0.015$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.120$$

Since $0.120 = 12.0\%$, and $12.0\% < 13\%$, the statement is True.
